differences.title: 1. ARCHITECTURE CORE
differences.leftDesc: TimescaleDB is an extension to PostgreSQL: hypertables, background jobs, and SQL planner integration all run inside Postgres, so queries, indexing, and transactions follow PostgreSQL semantics and tooling.
differences.rightDesc: QuestDB is a purpose-built time-series database optimized around columnar ingestion and query execution. It focuses on fast parsing, vectorized processing, and tight loops rather than reusing a full relational optimizer core.

differences.title: 2. INGESTION PATH
differences.leftDesc: In TimescaleDB, writes land in a hypertable and are routed to underlying time partitions (chunks). Continuous aggregation and compression policies run asynchronously via background workers to keep ingestion smooth.
differences.rightDesc: QuestDB ingests into partitioned column structures optimized for append-heavy workloads. It uses an ingestion pipeline designed for minimal per-row overhead, emphasizing bulk-friendly parsing and immediate column materialization.

differences.title: 3. PARTITIONING MODEL
differences.leftDesc: TimescaleDB creates hypertables that map to many chunks. Each chunk has its own indexes and can be compressed or dropped independently, enabling retention and fast pruning using time-based constraints.
differences.rightDesc: QuestDB partitions data to keep column scans and aggregations localized. Query engines can skip partitions based on time predicates, while column layouts aim to improve cache locality during aggregation.

differences.title: 4. QUERY ENGINE & EXECUTION
differences.leftDesc: TimescaleDB leverages PostgreSQL’s optimizer and executor. It can push down predicates, use standard B-tree/GiST indexes, and compose joins/CTEs—then benefits from hypertable chunk exclusion and time-aware planning.
differences.rightDesc: QuestDB uses a native execution engine oriented around vectorized operations. It attempts to process batches of rows/values at once to reduce function-call overhead and accelerate aggregations and filters over compressed columns.

differences.title: 5. COMPRESSION & RETENTION
differences.leftDesc: TimescaleDB supports column-level compression per chunk, typically using ordering and dictionaries appropriate for time-series patterns. Compression can be applied automatically by policies, paired with automated retention drops.
differences.rightDesc: QuestDB stores data in compact column representations and applies optimizations suited for telemetry characteristics. Retention and downsampling are designed to reduce scan volume by keeping historical data in efficient on-disk formats.

differences.title: 6. AGGREGATIONS & MATERIALIZATION
differences.leftDesc: TimescaleDB provides continuous aggregates that incrementally refresh materialized summaries. Jobs track watermarks per aggregate, updating only new data and avoiding full-table recomputation for dashboards.
differences.rightDesc: QuestDB offers mechanisms for rollups/downsampling by designing queries and storage patterns that precompute common windows. The execution engine is tuned to compute grouped metrics efficiently across large time ranges.

differences.title: 7. ECOSYSTEM & OPERABILITY
differences.leftDesc: Because TimescaleDB is PostgreSQL-based, you inherit Postgres operational tooling: pg_stat views, logical replication options, backup/restore patterns, and mature extensions. Integrating with existing SQL workflows is straightforward.
differences.rightDesc: QuestDB is focused on telemetry workflows with purpose-built ingestion and query endpoints. Operational patterns can differ from Postgres-centric stacks, but it’s designed to minimize moving parts for event/log-style time-series workloads.
